The transfer matrix of this long-wavelength theory follows from the real-space Dirac equation. To pass to real space, we perform the canonical replacement p\rightarrow-\mathrm{i}\mathrm{d}/\mathrm{d}x. The Schrödinger equation H_{\mathrm{D}}\psi=E\psi becomes

\left(-\mathrm{i}\gamma\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}+m\right)\psi(x)=E\psi(x). (16)

This equation can be written as

\frac{\mathrm{d}\psi}{\mathrm{d}x}(x)=\mathrm{i}\gamma^{-1}(E-m)\psi(x). (17)

Thus, propagation in space is generated by

\psi(x+\Delta)=e^{\mathrm{i}\gamma^{-1}(E-m)\Delta}\psi(x),\qquad\hat{T}(E):=e^{\mathrm{i}\gamma^{-1}(E-m)}. (18)

In this sense, \hat{T}(E) is the transfer matrix of the Dirac theory: it propagates the wavefunction in continuous real space by a unit of distance. Its eigenvalues are of the form e^{\mathrm{i}k(E)}, so that the operator \hat{k}(E)=\gamma^{-1}(E-m) gives the allowed momenta as functions of energy. Real values of k(E) describe propagating modes – plane waves – while complex values of k(E) describe modes that grow or decay in space – evanescent waves.

As a first example, we consider the minimal two-band Dirac Hamiltonian with \gamma=\sigma_{y} and m=\sigma_{x}, where \sigma_{x} and \sigma_{y} are Pauli matrices. We show the momentum spectrum resulting from diagonalising \hat{k}(E) in Fig. 1, where we plot k_{j}(E) horizontally and E vertically to conform with the usual convention for band structures. We call each k_{j}(E) a momentum branch. Where an eigenvalue k_{j} satisfies \mathrm{Im}\,k_{j}(E)=0, we call it a real-momentum branch; if \mathrm{Re}\,k_{j}(E)=0, we call it an imaginary-momentum branch. We combine the real and imaginary parts of the same momentum branches in the three-dimensional plot shown in Fig. 1c.

The 3D plot in Fig. 1c allows us to follow the momentum branches continuously as the energy is varied. With \gamma=\sigma_{y} and m=\sigma_{x}, these branches are

k_{\pm}(E)=\pm\sqrt{E^{2}-1}. (19)

For |E|>1, the two branches are real and reproduce the usual real-momentum spectrum. At the lower-energy band edge, E=-1, the two real-momentum branches meet at k=0. For -1<E<1, they continue as

k_{j}(E)=\pm\mathrm{i}\sqrt{1-E^{2}},\quad j\in\{1,2\}, (20)

and therefore lie on the imaginary-k axis. At the upper-energy band edge, E=1, the reverse process occurs: the two imaginary-momentum branches meet again at k=0 and continue as real-momentum branches as energy is increased.

The coalescence points at E=\pm 1 are exceptional points of the transfer matrix: we have

\hat{T}(\pm 1)=\mathbb{1}_{2\times 2}+N_{\pm},\qquad N_{\pm}=\mathrm{i}\sigma_{y}(\pm\mathbb{1}_{2\times 2}-\sigma_{x}), (21)

with

N_{\pm}^{2}=0,\qquad N_{\pm}\neq 0. (22)

Thus \hat{T}(\pm 1)-\mathbb{1}_{2\times 2} has a one-dimensional kernel: the two coincident eigenvalues share only one linearly independent eigenvector. This is the defining property of an exceptional point. The explicit calculation above should not be viewed as a peculiarity of the chosen Pauli matrices. Intuitively, the two colliding branches belong to the same band, and as they merge, both corresponding transfer-matrix eigenvectors approach the one associated with the single Bloch state at the band extremum, so that they coalesce and the transfer matrix becomes defective. A general proof, formulated directly in terms of the transfer matrix, is given in Appendix B.

An interesting feature emerges when two imaginary-momentum branches coalesce: exceptional points appear inside the gap. To illustrate this, we next consider a four-band model constructed from two coupled two-band systems given by

\displaystyle\gamma \displaystyle=\mathbb{1}_{2}\otimes\sigma_{y}, (23)
\displaystyle m \displaystyle=a\mathbb{1}_{2}\otimes\sigma_{x}+b\sigma_{y}\otimes\sigma_{y}+c\sigma_{z}\otimes\sigma_{x},

for different real values a,b and c. In this construction, imaginary-momentum branches associated with different band edges can coalesce inside the gap. The corresponding spectrum is shown in Fig. 2 and reads

\displaystyle k(E)= \displaystyle\pm\sqrt{E^{2}-a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2}\pm 2\Delta(E)}, (24)
\displaystyle\Delta(E)\equiv \displaystyle\sqrt{b^{2}(E^{2}-a^{2})+a^{2}c^{2}}.

Compared to the two-band model, the momentum spectrum now contains two pairs of imaginary-momentum branches, originating from two band edges. The separation between these two pairs is controlled by \Delta(E). When \Delta(E)\neq 0, the two pairs are distinct. When \Delta(E)=0, the two choices of the inner sign in Eq. (24) coincide, so different imaginary-momentum branches coalesce at the same energy.
